title: The strategic risk leader: building the capabilities that define the next decade in consulting
summary: Risk leadership in consulting firms is changing. See the data, Governed AI, and strategy capabilities risk leaders need to build for the next decade.
body_markdown:
The most effective risk leaders in consulting and advisory firms over the next decade will look considerably different from the most effective risk leaders today. The firms that recognize this early and invest accordingly will have a durable advantage. The capabilities required to lead risk at scale, across complex, private equity (PE)-backed, globally operating consulting firms, are expanding fast, and the profession is only at the beginning of that shift.


## A broader mandate


For decades, the most important qualifications for a risk leader in a consulting firm were professional judgment, regulatory knowledge relevant to the firm’s client base, and the credibility to say no to senior partners. These remain necessary. They are no longer sufficient.


Consulting firms face a range of regulatory obligations that carry genuine consequences. Still, the governance of conflicts of interest, client acceptance integrity, and information barriers rests on the firm’s own systems and culture. That places the risk leader in a position of real consequence: the person whose systems and judgment determine whether the firm can see, manage, and prove what’s accumulating across its portfolio.


The firms leading on risk today are finding and developing leaders who connect risk intelligence to business strategy, operate confidently in a data-driven environment, and treat Governed AI as a core firm function. The result is a risk function that actively supports growth, earns credibility with boards and PE investors, and positions the firm as demonstrably well-governed to sophisticated clients in financial services, government, and highly regulated industries who, in our experience, increasingly make governance a qualification criterion.


## Today’s reality


Today’s consulting risk leaders must navigate capabilities that weren’t central to the role a decade ago.


- **Portfolio-level exposure management** : Real-time visibility into how risk accumulates across clients, industries, geographies, and affiliated entities. We see portfolio visibility as where risk functions are tested hardest: individual partners making decisions that seemed reasonable in isolation, with nobody having a view of the whole.
- **Auditability at scale:** In our experience, clients are increasingly asking firms to demonstrate their conflicts processes, not just describe them. A firm whose conflicts history lives in email threads and institutional memory can’t answer that question credibly. The risk leader who has built a system that surfaces any decision, with its rationale and timestamp, on demand, is having a fundamentally different conversation with clients and regulators.
- **Information governance in practice:** As firms grow and serve increasingly complex client relationships across competing interests, the risk leader must own the information barrier infrastructure: not just the policy document, but the system that enforces it in practice. A documented wall that no one can verify is operating is not a wall.[Intapp Walls for AI](https://www.intapp.com/walls/) takes this further. It helps extend information barriers to AI tools and agents operating within the firm.
- **Governed AI:** As AI informs client work, engagement delivery, and compliance operations, the risk and compliance implications are inseparable from the firm’s broader risk posture. Governing how AI agents access and act on firm data is now a core risk management responsibility. Treating Governed AI as a separate initiative replicates the compartmentalized thinking of a function that works in silos.
- **Stakeholder communication:** In our experience, with PE investors, boards, and sophisticated clients expecting clearer articulation of how risk considerations influence strategy and client selection, the risk leader’s role has become significantly more externally facing. The ability to explain how risk insight shapes firm-level decisions is now a core expectation, and the risk leader who can demonstrate it with data has a different standing in those conversations than one who relies on narrative.


## Building the capability


Building the risk leadership capability that modern consulting firms need is a multi-year effort. The firms making the most progress are approaching it in three ways.


### **Investing in existing risk talent**


Today’s risk leaders need more than subject-matter expertise and policy knowledge. They need data analytics fluency, technology literacy, and the ability to translate data insight into decisions. Risk leaders developing proficiency in these skills alongside their governance expertise are building capabilities that compound as firms become more data-driven.


Innovation mindset matters here too. The risk leaders who will define the next decade are the ones who see agentic AI and connected data infrastructure as opportunities to fundamentally redesign how compliance functions operate, not just tools to marginally speed up existing processes. Firms that invest in developing these capabilities in experienced risk professionals, rather than waiting to hire them, build institutional knowledge that doesn’t walk out the door.


### **Integrating risk and data leadership**


In the most forward-leaning consulting firms, the risk function has closer structural relationships with data, technology, and operations leadership. Purpose-built platforms like[Intapp Intake](https://www.intapp.com/intake/) ,[Intapp Conflicts](https://www.intapp.com/conflicts/) ,[Intapp Employee Compliance](https://www.intapp.com/employee-compliance/) , and[Intapp Walls](https://www.intapp.com/walls/) help give risk leaders a connected data environment.


The value grows when solutions work together across the engagement lifecycle. Connecting risk intelligence to the earliest stage of client pursuit, through[Intapp DealCloud](https://www.intapp.com/dealcloud/) or a firm’s existing CRM, means screening for conflicts before relationship investment builds. Monitoring during active engagements through time-tracking data can surface early signals that manual oversight may miss.


[Intapp Celeste](https://www.intapp.com/celeste/) brings this together at the agentic layer. Celeste agents take on high-volume, process-intensive work so the team can focus on judgment calls.


Celeste’s[built-in playbooks](https://www.intapp.com/celeste/use-cases/?industry=consulting) are configured to each firm’s specific policies, decision logic, and data. Because the playbooks are pre-built and centrally governed, individual users across the firm don’t have to construct compliance processes from scratch, which drives consistency.


### **Building the next generation’s risk experience**


The managers and senior advisors who will lead risk functions over the next decade are in the firm now. Giving them exposure to portfolio-level risk decisions, data governance work, AI governance challenges, and the design of compliance systems, rather than compliance review alone, determines whether the talent pipeline is ready when it needs to be.


## Positioning risk upstream


There’s a deeper question underneath the skills conversation: where does the risk function sit in the firm’s decision-making architecture?


A portfolio manager who only reports performance after positions have moved isn’t managing a portfolio. A risk function positioned purely as a control mechanism, downstream from strategy and focused on review and documentation, has the same problem. The consulting firms that will lead on risk over the next decade are repositioning the function upstream, where it informs client selection, pricing, capacity decisions, and investment priorities before commitments are made.


For PE-backed firms, we see this as table stakes. We are told that investors who expect EBITDA improvement alongside growth look at the compliance operating model as a signal of operational maturity. A risk function that runs on email and manual processes is a liability in that conversation. A risk function that can demonstrate real-time portfolio visibility, auditable decisions, and an agentic AI capability that helps the function scale is an asset.


The risk leader who can say[‘our compliance posture is a competitive advantage](https://www.intapp.com/blog/risk-intelligence-consulting-firms/) , and here is the evidence’ stands in a stronger position with the partnership, the board, and prospective clients than the risk leader defending an email-based process and hoping the next near-miss doesn’t become a crisis.


In a profession where reputation is the primary asset, a risk function that earns the confidence of partners, clients, and investors is the infrastructure that makes sustained growth possible.
